one_liner: Go port of simdjson's SIMD parser for AVX2 amd64; builds a navigable tape 2.3-16.5x faster than encoding/json's interface{} decode.
what_it_does: Parses an in-memory JSON object or array with Parse, or NDJSON with ParseND or ParseNDStream (from an io.Reader), into simdjson's flat tape format. You then read it through an iterator API: Iter, Object and Array, path lookup with FindElement, ForEach with key filters, typed getters such as Int, Float and StringBytes, and AsFloat, AsInteger or AsString for homogeneous arrays. It is not a drop-in for encoding/json: the README says it cannot unmarshal into structs, and Iter.Interface() or Object.Map() build interface{}/map values with an allocation per element. It can also replace scalar values in place, delete object or array elements, re-marshal any subtree to JSON, and serialize the parsed tape to a compact binary form (s2 or zstd) that can be read back even on CPUs the parser does not support.
how_it_is_fast: Stage 1 is simdjson's structural-indexing algorithm, translated from C intrinsics to Go assembly with c2goasm: for each 64-byte block it finds odd-length backslash runs, builds the in-string mask with a carry-less-multiply prefix-XOR (VPCLMULQDQ), classifies whitespace and structural characters with AVX2 (an AVX-512 variant is picked at runtime when AVX512F is present), and flattens the bitmask into uint32 incremental offsets. Stage 2 is a goto-based state machine in Go that consumes those offsets and writes a []uint64 tape with skip pointers over objects and arrays; it validates and unescapes strings in AVX2 assembly, and with WithCopyStrings(false) leaves them pointing into the input. For inputs over 8 KB the two stages run concurrently on two goroutines connected by a channel, and reusing the previous ParsedJson keeps each parse to a few dozen allocations. Numbers go through scalar strconv.ParseInt/ParseFloat rather than SIMD, which is why number-heavy files gain the least.
when_to_use: Large in-memory documents (over 8 KB, so the two stages overlap) or NDJSON streams on x86-64 servers with AVX2+CLMUL (Intel Haswell or later, AMD Zen or later), where parse throughput is the bottleneck.

Pulling a few fields out of big, string- or structure-heavy payloads such as event feeds, API dumps or logs without building Go values, using FindElement or Object.ForEach with an onlyKeys filter. This input shape got 6.5-16.5x over encoding/json in the README table (twitter 11.3x, citm_catalog 12.5x, gsoc-2018 16.5x).

Filtering or rewriting NDJSON: ParseNDStream splits an io.Reader into ~10 MB chunks and parses them on (GOMAXPROCS+1)/2 goroutines, and DeleteElems, the Set* methods and MarshalJSON let you edit records and write them back out.

Storing parsed JSON for repeated reads. The Serializer shrank parking-citations-1M to 10.9-17.2% of the JSON size with compression and deserializes at 806-2334 MB/s (README), and it deserializes on any CPU.
when_not_to_use: You need struct binding or a drop-in Unmarshal. It has none, and converting the tape into your own structs or interface{} is extra work that the headline benchmark leaves out. In issue #91 a Nostr client was 5.5x slower than encoding/json (53.1 vs 9.6 ms) until it reused ParsedJson/Object/Array values. After that it was only modestly ahead of easyjson (8.1 vs 9.8 ms).

arm64 (Graviton, Apple Silicon), 386, gccgo, noasm/appengine builds, or x86 CPUs without AVX2+CLMUL. Parse returns 'Unsupported platform' or 'Host CPU does not meet target specs', with no pure-Go fallback, and a maintainer said an arm64 port 'will probably not be done in the scope of this project' (#51).

Number-heavy data (GeoJSON coordinates, meshes, numeric arrays): canada, marine_ik, mesh, mesh.pretty and numbers gained only 2.3-3.9x over encoding/json in the README table, because number conversion is scalar strconv.

Tiny messages, top-level scalars, or one giant array that does not fit in memory. A fresh parser carries ~96 KB of stage-1 index buffers plus a tape pre-sized to about 1.2x the input bytes. Parse rejects top-level null, true, false, numbers and strings (#59). It cannot lazily stream one huge array; only NDJSON streams (#87).

Untrusted input where strict validation matters. Open issue #96 (2026-07-31, unanswered) reports that \u escapes containing bytes 0x00-0x2F are accepted as digit 0: the digittoval DATA table in parse_string_amd64.s does skip offsets 0x40-0x6F. It also reports that the string-scan bound is passed to the assembly by address, so an unterminated string can be read past the intended window.

integration.dependencies: github.com/klauspost/cpuid/v2 v2.2.10, github.com/klauspost/compress v1.18.0 (golang.org/x/sys indirect); no cgo
integration.min_toolchain: Go 1.22 per go.mod; CI tests 1.22.x-1.24.x; gc toolchain only (gccgo cannot build the Go assembly and reports an unsupported CPU)
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AVX2 + CLMUL required (an AVX-512F stage-1 path is selected at runtime when available); other GOARCH values compile, but Parse, ParseND and ParseNDStream return an error; Serializer.Deserialize works everywhere
integration.thread_safety: Mostly not documented. Separate Parse calls with separate ParsedJson values are independent (the repo's nocopy-par benchmark runs one per goroutine). A ParsedJson passed as `reuse` is overwritten. A source comment says a Serializer 'can be reused, but not used concurrently'.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false — different API (a tape plus iterators; no struct Unmarshal). Iter.Interface() and Object.Map() give interface{}/map[string]interface{} results, but they allocate per element and are not part of the benchmarked path.

gotchas: WithCopyStrings(false) is the fast mode (Twitter 1327 vs 1073 MB/s in the README) but makes tape strings point into your input slice, so the buffer must stay alive and unmodified while the ParsedJson is in use. The default copies strings.

Always pass the previous *ParsedJson as `reuse`, since fresh parsers allocate index buffers and a tape every call. ParseND does not attach its internal parser to the returned value (Parse does), so reuse is largely ineffective for ParseND.

The latest tag, v0.4.5 (2023-03-13), is what `go get` resolves. It lacks later master fixes, including #92 (merged 2025-06-16): Object.ForEach with an onlyKeys filter consumed the next key after skipping a value. Pin a commit pseudo-version if you use that API.

Parse runs its two stages on two goroutines for inputs over 8 KB, so a per-call MB/s figure can use two cores while encoding/json uses one. Separately, the serializer uses //go:linkname to runtime.memhash, which ties it to Go runtime internals across toolchain upgrades.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Over fastjson (valyala), which also parses into its own untyped value, pick simdjson-go for large or NDJSON input read from an io.Reader (fastjson's README says it cannot parse from a Reader, while ParseNDStream parses chunks in parallel) or when you want a compact binary serialized form. Pick Sonic, jsoniter or easyjson instead when you need to decode into Go structs, and Sonic also when you need arm64 (Go 1.20+).
verified_claims_summary: The README's benchcmp table compares simdjson.Parse building its tape (strings copied, ParsedJson reused) against encoding/json.Unmarshal into interface{} on 14 standard corpus files: speedups run from 2.34x (numbers) to 16.50x (gsoc-2018), with a geometric mean of ~6.4x, so the '10x' headline overstates the table, and the two sides do different work. A maintainer comment on issue #35 (2021-05-17) says the numbers came from an AMD Ryzen 3950 with Go 1.16.2 (GOMAXPROCS=32, and Parse overlaps its two stages on two goroutines for these >8 KB files); the table has not been re-run since.
status_note: Stale (last commit 2025-08-26, last tag v0.4.5 from March 2023; maintainers called it 'purpose built' and done in #86 and have not answered a July 2026 offer, #96, of fixes, ~35% faster parsing and a portable path from the data-bet fork), but it is Apache-2.0 pure Go plus assembly with two small dependencies, so it is easy to vendor or fork, and minio/minio (now archived) pins v0.4.5.
